title: Deterministic Quantum Events on a Dual-Axis State Bundle: A Falsifiable Recurrence Test of Single-Event Continuity
content: The Born rule assigns a probability law to a physical state and a complete observation state, but a probability law is not the event realized in one trial. Building on the physical–observation dual-axis state space, we construct an event layer that separates these two mathematical objects. Every measurable finite Born kernel admits a deterministic circle lift whose event cells have the required normalized Haar volumes. On a principal U(1) selector bundle, cell membership is gauge invariant and Haar reduction returns the Born trace law exactly. A gauge-invariant action yields both selector transport and an observation-axis equation in which mixed curvature is the cross-axis force. The Fisher metric of the Born response supplies its minimal kinetic geometry, while a least-interface principle fixes connected binary event cells. Curvature determines relative transport but cannot select an absolute event without an initial selector; pure principal transport preserves Haar equilibrium but cannot create it. Bell violation further requires the deterministic event map to be contextual on the implemented joint setting. The event law leads to a concrete test of single-event continuity. The physical control is an azimuthal cycle and the observation coordinate is calibrated independently from the binary Born response. The benchmark states three additional closures explicitly: a reduced spherical completion with rotationally invariant unit-Chern curvature, minimal free response dynamics, and a selector-transparent returning instrument. The fixed dimensionless protocol X = 0.100 and ωS/Ω = 4 has a unique balanced periodic response orbit and predicts the protocol constant κM = 0.03080966337. No event record enters this calculation. A returning measure-and-prepare instrument then predicts a triangular mismatch recurrence: 0.980702% after one cycle, 99.9684% after 102 cycles, and 0.0632% after 204 cycles, although every single-cycle marginal remains balanced. The memoryless realization of the same instrument gives 50% mismatch at every nonzero lag. Separate response, phase-calibration, and event ensembles prevent the predicted orbit from being programmed into the test, while causal-break and selector-scrambling controls bound ordinary apparatus memory. This numerical “M-event fingerprint” converts the century-old question of objective single-event continuity into a preregisterable, falsifiable serial-correlation experiment. It is a protocol-specific prediction, not a new natural constant; a null result falsifies the stated minimal realization rather than every possible deterministic completion.
